prints.event: Canada Consumer Price Index, September (Statistics Canada)
prints.read: A touch cooler than expected and all energy: gasoline is up 27.8% on the year while CPI excluding gasoline runs 2.2% and the core measures slipped (CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%, common 2.4%), so the Bank of Canada holds at 2.25% on October 28 and the Canadian dollar firmed to a four-week high; for US rates it is a small vote that the oil shock is not spreading into core.

A clear miss and the lowest reading since June 2012: present sales 33 (down 2), six-month expectations 32 (down 5), buyer traffic 18 (down 5, lowest since April 2012 outside the pandemic month), 43% of builders cutting prices with the 30-year mortgage at 7.40%; it argues the 5% ten-year is already biting on housing, which is a growth-negative that helps the front end more than it hurts stocks today.

No consensus found; auctions close at 10:30 CT (not yet held at the time of writing) and the 26-week stop staying well above the 13-week keeps the December hike priced, while a narrower gap after this morning's housing miss would say the market is trimming it.

prints.event: China GDP, third quarter (NBS, released Sunday evening CT)
prints.read: A small beat on the year-on-year rate with the quarter-on-quarter pace at 1.2%, enough to steady Asia and support US futures overnight but not a growth story on its own.
In line; factory output is holding up while property investment is down 20.6% year to date and the surveyed urban jobless rate sits at 5.2%.
The clearest beat of the batch, though a 1% consumer is still weak and investment is the drag.

prints.event: China fixed-asset investment, January to September (NBS)
prints.read: The miss in the batch; investment is contracting faster than expected with property down 20.6%, which caps how much the GDP beat helps commodities and industrial names.

read.call: A relief bounce in the beaten-up chip and AI names (Nasdaq up about 0.9%, S&P up about 0.4%, VIX down 9% to 18 by mid-morning) with oil off $2 and the housing miss giving bonds a reason not to sell, so the day leans higher but on thin conviction with no Fed speakers and the real tests (Netflix, GE Aerospace and the rest of the earnings week) not until tomorrow.
read.swing: The ten-year yield, sitting near 5.11% to 5.13% and up a few basis points on the day: a push back through last week's highs around 5.20% turns the tech bounce into another sale, while a bid after the NAHB miss and the 10:30 bill auctions lets it run.
drivers: Builder sentiment fell to 29, the lowest since June 2012, with buyer traffic at 18 and 43% of builders cutting prices; the first hard sign the 5% ten-year and 7.40% mortgage are hitting activity.
Canada's September CPI came in at 3.1% y/y, under the 3.2% consensus, with core measures easing to 1.8% to 1.9%; the energy shock is not yet spreading into core north of the border.
Brent is down about 1.7% to around $108 and WTI near $100.50 as Middle East supply holds near pre-war levels despite three tankers damaged in the Strait of Hormuz.
Chips and AI names are bouncing after the Nasdaq lost about 4.5% last week and semis posted their longest losing streak since 2008; Intel is up near 5% on a JPMorgan upgrade.

Fed blackout through October 29 after Chair Warsh gave no steer on the October 28 decision; markets price roughly an 83% hold next week and a 75% to 90% chance of a December hike depending on the source.

what_mattered.headline: Builder confidence hits a 14-year low
what_mattered.fact: NAHB index 29 in October versus 31 expected and 32 prior; buyer traffic 18, expectations 32 (down 5), 43% of builders cut prices, average cut 6%.
what_mattered.implication: Housing is the first sector to show the rate shock in the hard-ish data; it supports the front end and weighs on builders and building-products names, and it gives the Fed a growth argument against a December hike.

what_mattered.headline: Canada inflation cooler than feared, core easing
what_mattered.fact: CPI 3.1% y/y (consensus 3.2%), 0.1% m/m NSA; gasoline up 27.8% y/y, CPI ex-gasoline 2.2%, CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%.
what_mattered.implication: Bank of Canada holds at 2.25% on October 28 and the Canadian dollar made a four-week high; a data point for the view that the oil shock stays a headline, not a core, problem.

what_mattered.headline: Tech bounce with yields still above 5%
what_mattered.implication: A positioning bounce after last week's sell-off rather than a change in the rate picture; the Dow's industrial and housing names are not participating.

what_mattered.headline: China Q3 GDP beats, investment misses
what_mattered.fact: GDP 4.5% y/y (consensus 4.4%), retail sales 1.1% (consensus 0.5%), fixed-asset investment -7.2% year to date (consensus -6.5%), property investment -20.6%.
what_mattered.implication: Steadied Asia overnight but the investment contraction limits the read-through to commodities and industrials.

look_at: The 10:30 CT 13-week and 26-week bill stops: last week's 4.085% and 4.200% embed a December hike, so watch whether the 26-week stop drifts lower after the housing miss.
The ten-year around 5.11% to 5.13%: the tech bounce only survives the afternoon if the long end stays under last week's highs near 5.20%.
Homebuilders and building products after the NAHB print: a weak close in that group with the broad tape up confirms the market is reading it as a sector problem, not a macro turn.
Oil near $108 Brent with three tankers damaged in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend: any renewed spike reverses today's bid in bonds and tech.
Tomorrow's set-up: Netflix, GE Aerospace, GM and Capital One report, the Atlanta Fed GDPNow updates from 3.6% at 10:00 CT, and no Fed speakers until the October 28 decision.

fed.market_pricing: Fed funds 3.75% to 4.00% after the September 16 hike. Markets price roughly an 83% hold on October 28 (October hike odds about 15% after Warsh's Bangkok remarks) and a December 9 hike at 75% to over 90% depending on the source (Trading Economics about 75%, FXStreet citing CME FedWatch over 90%).
speakers_today: None scheduled: FOMC blackout runs through October 29. The Board holds a closed meeting at 10:30 CT with no public remarks; the Board calendar lists only statistical releases (CP at 12:00 CT, H.10 and H.15 at 15:15 CT).

themes: Is the rate shock reaching the real economy: builder sentiment at 29, the lowest since 2012, with buyer traffic at 18 says yes for housing, while the 3.6% GDPNow says not yet for the whole economy.
Does the oil shock spread into core: Canada's September print says no so far (headline 3.1%, core 1.8% to 1.9%), the opposite of last week's hot US CPI and PPI.
A December hike is still the base case at 75% to 90% priced, but today's weak housing data and softer oil are the first two arguments against it since the Chair spoke on Friday.
